entities.summary:
Guillaume André Villoteau was a French musicologist who made significant contributions to the understanding of opera in 19th-century France. His work, particularly his study of Gluck's influence on Mozart, had a lasting impact on the field of musicology. Villoteau's research also explored the role of opera in shaping French culture and society during the Napoleonic era. His writings on the subject were widely read and admired by his contemporaries, including notable figures such as Hector Berlioz and Franz Liszt. Villoteau's legacy as a musicologist continues to be felt today, with his work serving as a foundation for future research on the history of opera.

Villoteau was born in Bellême, France, on September 19, 1759, and died in Paris on April 27, 1839. His early life and education were marked by a strong interest in music and literature, which he pursued through his studies at the École des Beaux-Arts. After completing his studies, Villoteau went on to serve as a professor of musicology at the Sorbonne, where he taught courses on music history and theory.

Villoteau's work as a musicologist was not limited to his academic pursuits. He was also a prolific writer and critic, whose reviews and articles appeared in numerous publications, including the influential music journal, Le Musique.

Despite his significant contributions to the field of musicology, Villoteau's work has largely been overlooked in recent years. However, his legacy as a pioneering musicologist continues to be celebrated by scholars and music lovers alike.

In conclusion, Guillaume André Villoteau was a remarkable figure in the history of musicology, whose groundbreaking research and writings had a lasting impact on our understanding of opera in 19th-century France. His legacy serves as a testament to the power of scholarship and the importance of preserving our cultural heritage.
